title: Philosophy
text: Principles shaped by building decision systems that must be trusted, explainable, and durable. These are not abstract ideas—they are patterns that consistently lead to reliable outcomes in environments where decisions carry operational, financial, or clinical consequences.

title: Philosophy
section: Model the Decision, Not the Dataset
text:
Model the Decision, Not the Dataset
Effective systems begin with a clear understanding of the decision being made, the constraints surrounding it, and the risks of getting it wrong. Data serves as an input, not the anchor. A model produces a prediction; a system produces a decision. My focus is on the latter.
Key considerations include:

The structure of the decision: Mapping how a choice is actually executed in the field.
The incentives and failure modes: Identifying what happens when the system is wrong and who bears the cost.
The operational environment: Designing for the specific latency and throughput requirements of the business.

This orientation ensures solutions align with real-world decision dynamics rather than purely statistical elegance.

title: Philosophy
text:
Reduce Ambiguity Before Increasing Complexity
Ambiguity is the enemy of reliability. Before expanding feature sets or exploring advanced architectures, the foundation must be clarified:

Defining “Good”: Establishing gold-standard labels that reflect business reality, not just available data.
Defining Failure: Explicitly documenting what constitutes a system-level error versus a tolerable model variance.
Identifying Constraints: Surfacing regulatory or technical limits before they become architectural bottlenecks.

Clear definitions early on prevent downstream reliability issues and create a stable base for technical work.

title: Philosophy
text:
Design for Reliability, Not Cleverness
High-stakes systems must be predictable, auditable, and robust under pressure. Reliability takes precedence over novelty.
Core practices include:

Interpretability Over “Black Boxes”: Prioritizing models that stakeholders can trust and auditors can verify.
Deterministic Guardrails: Wrapping probabilistic models in deterministic rules to ensure safety at the “edges”.
Fail-Safe Design: Ensuring systems are designed to fail safely toward human expertise, not away from it.

The objective is dependable performance, not algorithmic experimentation.

title: Philosophy
text:
Treat Constraints as Features
Regulatory requirements, workflow bottlenecks, and human review patterns are integral components of system design. Incorporating these constraints early produces solutions that integrate cleanly into real-world environments and withstand scrutiny.

title: Philosophy
text:
Make Uncertainty a First-Class Signal
Uncertainty is quantified explicitly and used to guide safe fallback paths, escalation logic, and human-in-the-loop review. Systems built with uncertainty in mind behave predictably even when data conditions shift.

title: Philosophy
text:
Technical Foundations Behind the Philosophy
These principles translate into concrete engineering practices that support reliability in production:

Economic-Metric Alignment: Developing evaluation metrics that map directly to P&L or clinical safety outcomes.
Scenario-Based Testing: Stress-testing systems against edge cases and adversarial patterns before deployment.
Hybrid Architectures: Blending rules-based logic with machine learning to balance interpretability and precision.
Audit-First Lifecycle: Implementing versioning and “decision-tracing” to ensure every action is explainable years later.
Data Quality as a Lever: Treating data pipelines as a core reliability component, not just a plumbing task.

title: Philosophy
text:
What This Philosophy Enables
These principles consistently produce systems that:

Improve decision quality without increasing operational burden.
Hold up under regulatory and audit scrutiny.
Scale across teams, workflows, and product surfaces.
Build trust with stakeholders who depend on the outcomes.

title: Expertise
text: Expertise shaped by building decision systems in regulated, high‑stakes environments. The focus is on reliability, clarity, and operational fit—ensuring that models, rules, and workflows behave predictably under real-world constraints.

title: Expertise
text:

Designing systems that encode decisions, not just predictions. This includes structuring how data, rules, and models interact to support consistent, auditable outcomes.
Areas of depth:

Translating business decisions into formal decision logic

Structuring systems for transparency, fallback behavior, and human review

title: Expertise
text:
Modeling and Statistical Methods
Applying statistical and machine learning techniques with an emphasis on interpretability, robustness, and operational alignment.
Capabilities include:

Supervised learning for classification, ranking, and risk scoring

Probabilistic modeling and uncertainty quantification

Feature engineering grounded in domain constraints

Model evaluation using decision-aligned metrics rather than generic benchmarks

The emphasis is on models that perform reliably in production, not just in experimentation.

title: Expertise
text:
Data Quality and Signal Integrity
High-stakes systems depend on stable, trustworthy data. Expertise includes designing processes that ensure data remains usable, consistent, and meaningful over time.
Focus areas:

Upstream validation and schema stability

Monitoring for drift, staleness, and signal degradation

Designing guardrails for missing, delayed, or corrupted data

Building resilience into pipelines that feed decision systems

These practices reduce operational surprises and support long-term reliability.

title: Expertise
text:
Workflow and Product Integration
Decision systems must integrate cleanly into the environments where people work. Expertise includes aligning technical solutions with real operational constraints.
Examples of integration work:

Designing thresholds, review queues, and escalation paths

Mapping model outputs to user actions and workflow steps

Reducing friction for clinicians, investigators, or compliance teams

Ensuring systems enhance—not disrupt—existing processes

This alignment increases adoption and improves decision quality.

title: Expertise
text:
Monitoring, Governance, and Lifecycle Management
Long-term durability requires systems that can be monitored, audited, and evolved without losing trust.
Core capabilities:

Designing monitoring frameworks for drift, performance, and data quality

Implementing versioning, rollback, and change‑management processes

Creating audit trails that satisfy regulatory and internal governance needs

Structuring lifecycle plans for models, rules, and decision logic

These practices ensure systems remain reliable years after deployment.

title: Expertise
text:
Cross‑Functional Alignment and Communication
Effective decision systems require alignment across technical, operational, and regulatory stakeholders. Expertise includes translating ambiguity into structured decisions and driving clarity across teams.
Strengths include:

Framing tradeoffs and constraints in accessible terms

Aligning engineering, product, and domain experts around shared goals

Communicating risk, uncertainty, and system behavior clearly

Supporting decision-making processes with structured analysis

This capability accelerates adoption and reduces organizational friction.

title: Expertise
text:
Domains of Application
These capabilities have been applied across multiple high‑stakes domains:

Fraud detection — risk scoring, anomaly detection, hybrid rules‑plus‑ML systems

Clinical workflow optimization — triage logic, prioritization systems, operational decision support

Compliance automation — rule encoding, exception handling, audit‑ready decision pipelines

Each domain reinforces the same core principles: clarity, reliability, and operational fit.

title: Probabilistic Retention Intervention System
text:
Decision Context
Attrition prediction is only useful when it changes retention decisions. In practice, leaders need a calibrated way to decide who to intervene on, when to act, and what actions are justified given limited budget and manager capacity.
This project reframes attrition modeling into a decision-support system for targeted retention interventions.



The Core Decision
Given employee signals and a predicted attrition risk, which employees should receive intervention, what type of intervention is appropriate, and how should thresholds shift as capacity changes?
Constraints considered:

Limited HR and manager bandwidth

Intervention cost versus expected retention benefit

Risk of unfair or biased targeting

Need for transparent rationale




Approach

Built a probability-based attrition risk model

Focused on calibration and ranking rather than a single yes/no label

Designed threshold bands aligned to action levels:

Monitor
Manager check-in
Retention package / role adjustment


Highlighted driver visibility so actions can be justified and audited

Framed evaluation in terms of decision utility, not just accuracy




System Pattern

Ingest HR and performance signals

Validate and standardize inputs

Score attrition probability

Rank employees by risk and expected intervention value

Apply action thresholds based on capacity and cost

Log decisions and top drivers for review

This pattern supports responsible retention decisions at scale.



What This Demonstrates

Turning prediction into intervention policy

Capacity-aware thresholding

Action band design (monitor vs intervene)

Transparent decision rationale for stakeholder trust

Pandas
Scikit-learn
Classification modeling
Model evaluation and calibration concepts

title: Financial Anomaly Triage Framework
text:
Decision Context
Financial reporting and transaction ecosystems generate a high volume of signals, but investigative capacity is limited. The practical problem is not “detect everything,” but to prioritize which entities or patterns deserve attention first, with defensible thresholds and traceable rationale.
This project reframes fraud detection as a triage decision system: identify suspicious patterns, rank risk, and define intervention boundaries.



The Decision Problem
Given a set of financial signals, which cases should be escalated for review?
Constraints that matter:

Limited investigation bandwidth

Asymmetric cost (missed fraud vs false escalation)

Auditability of why something was flagged

Stability under distribution shift and noisy data




Approach
This work focuses on risk triage rather than pure classification:

Profiled and engineered anomaly-relevant signals

Applied unsupervised / semi-supervised detection patterns to surface outliers

Designed a ranking strategy so review starts with highest-risk cases

Introduced threshold concepts (escalate, monitor, ignore) rather than a single cutoff

Emphasized explainable drivers (what contributed to escalation)




Architecture (High-Level)
A triage-ready pattern:

Ingest signals (financial metrics, derived ratios, behavioral indicators)

Validate and standardize features

Generate anomaly scores

Rank cases by risk

Apply intervention thresholds (review vs monitor)

Log decisions and drivers for traceability

This structure supports scale and governance even when labels are incomplete.



What This Demonstrates

Reframing fraud detection into operational triage

Threshold thinking (capacity-aware interventions)

Explainability through driver decomposition

Governance-ready decision logging patterns




Technical Stack
Python
Pandas
Scikit-learn
Anomaly detection patterns
Feature engineering and risk ranking

title: Clinical Access Routing Architecture
text:
Decision Context
Healthcare access decisions often operate under limited capacity, uneven resource distribution, and ambiguous eligibility rules. The challenge is not simply analyzing data, but structuring routing logic that allocates care access in a consistent and defensible manner.
This project explores how access data can inform structured clinical routing decisions under operational constraints.



The Decision Problem
Given patient attributes and contextual signals, how should access be prioritized?
Key considerations:

Limited provider capacity

Fairness and equitable allocation

Risk of delayed intervention

Transparency of routing criteria

The objective shifts from prediction to structured decision support.



Approach
This project began as exploratory analysis of healthcare access patterns, then evolved into a decision-framing exercise:

Identified access bottlenecks and priority indicators

Modeled probability signals for delayed access risk

Evaluated threshold strategies for intervention routing

Structured deterministic guardrails for safety constraints

Explored how hybrid rule + probability systems improve transparency

The focus was not model accuracy alone, but decision reliability.



Architectural Insight
A clinical routing system must:

Separate scoring logic from intervention policy

Make thresholds adjustable based on capacity

Preserve human oversight for ambiguous cases

Log decisions for auditability

This transforms exploratory modeling into decision architecture.



What This Enables

Structured triage decision support

Operational routing transparency

Capacity-aware prioritization

Safer deployment of predictive signals

Scikit-learn
Exploratory data analysis
Probability modeling

title: About
text:
I’m a Principal Data Scientist specializing in high‑stakes decision systems across regulated and operationally complex domains. My work focuses on building models and workflows that organizations can trust, especially when the cost of a wrong decision is high.
I approach data science by modeling the decision, not just the dataset. That means reducing ambiguity before increasing complexity, aligning statistical rigor with operational constraints, and designing systems that are reliable, explainable, and durable in real‑world environments.
My experience spans fraud detection, clinical workflow optimization, compliance automation, and risk‑aware modeling frameworks. Across these areas, I focus on measurable impact, auditability, and the ability for systems to operate under real constraints rather than idealized assumptions.
My background blends data science, risk modeling, and technical program management. That combination helps me align stakeholders, clarify requirements, and deliver systems that work beyond the prototype stage.

title: Credit Risk Threshold Design Framework
text:
Decision Context
Credit risk models are often evaluated on predictive accuracy alone. In practice, lenders must decide where to set approval thresholds, how to price risk, and how to balance growth against default exposure.
This project reframes loan default modeling into a structured credit decision framework.



The Core Decision
Given applicant financial signals and a predicted probability of default, where should approval thresholds be set to optimize portfolio performance while controlling downside risk?
Constraints considered:

Capital exposure and loss tolerance

Regulatory expectations

Growth versus risk trade-offs

Fair and consistent approval logic




Approach

Built a probability-based default prediction model

Emphasized ranking and score calibration rather than binary output

Modeled threshold bands such as:

Approve
Review
Decline


Considered how thresholds shift under different risk appetite scenarios

Focused on explainability of key risk drivers

The goal was to simulate real credit decision logic, not just produce a classifier.



System Pattern

Ingest applicant financial indicators

Validate and standardize features

Generate probability of default score

Rank applicants by risk

Apply approval thresholds aligned to risk appetite

Log decision rationale and top contributing factors

This pattern mirrors modern credit portfolio design practices.



What This Demonstrates

Risk-adjusted threshold design

Portfolio-aware decision framing

Trade-off modeling between approval rate and loss exposure

Explainable scoring logic

Scikit-learn
Classification modeling
Probability calibration concepts
